summary: Describes the APEX access service, found at the well-known endpoint named apex=access. It controls who may use the APEX relaying mesh and other APEX services. The protocol is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: In a postal service, someone has to decide who may send mail. The access service was APEX's gatekeeper. It is historic now.

questions: what is the apex access service
can you use wildcards in access entries
how does a relay check permissions
subtitle: Controls who can use APEX relays and send messages to specific endpoints.

tldr.problem: APEX relays need a way to enforce fine-grained rules about which endpoints can send data to which other endpoints, and which services can be invoked.
tldr.mechanism: The access service manages access entries that specify an owner endpoint, an actor (sender) that may be wildcarded, and a list of permitted actions. Relays consult these entries when processing data messages.
tldr.outcome: The service was designed as a crucial part of APEX but, like APEX itself, never saw real deployment and is now historic.

today: RFC 3341 is now Historic. It was published as a critical companion to RFC 3340, the APEX core, but APEX never achieved adoption. The access service design is sophisticated but no longer in use.

sections.title: The Access Service: Gatekeeper for APEX
sections.content:
The APEX access service is built on top of the APEX core (RFC 3340) and serves as the gatekeeper for the relaying mesh. It controls two things: who can use the APEX relaying service, and which endpoints can send to which other endpoints.

Within each administrative domain, the access service is a well-known endpoint addressed as apex=access@domain.com. Applications and relays communicate with it by sending APEX data messages containing queries, get requests, or set operations. The service responds with allow/deny decisions, access entry information, or confirmations.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the access service as a registry that keeps track of permission rules. When a program tries to send a message, the relay checks with this service to see if it is allowed.

sections.title: Access Entries: Owner, Actor, and Actions
sections.content:
An access entry is the basic unit of control. Each entry has four parts:

Owner: the endpoint that owns the entry (for example, fred@example.com). Actor: the entity seeking to perform an action (for example, barney@example.com). The actor field supports limited wildcarding: barney/*@example.com matches any subaddress of Barney, *@example.com matches any endpoint in the domain, and *@*.example.com matches any endpoint in the domain or its subdomains.

Actions: a list of service/operation pairs (for example, core:data to send data through the relaying mesh, or presence:subscribe to subscribe to the presence service). lastUpdate: a timestamp showing when the entry was created or last modified.
sections.plainLanguage: An access entry says: 'Fred allows Barney to send him messages'. It has a timestamp so you know when the rule was made.

sections.title: Three Operations: Query, Get, and Set
sections.content:
Applications interact with the access service using three operations.

Query asks: 'Is action X allowed for actor Y with respect to owner Z?' The service consults the matching access entry and responds with allow or deny. The matching process uses the most specific entry that applies, preferring exact matches over wildcards.

Get retrieves an access entry, usually in preparation for updating it. The caller must already have permission to access the entry. Set creates, updates, or deletes an entry. Creating a new entry does not require a previous timestamp, but updating or deleting an entry requires the current timestamp to ensure atomic updates and prevent lost edits.
sections.plainLanguage: Query is like asking 'am I allowed to do this?'. Get is like 'show me the current rules'. Set is like 'change the rules'.

sections.title: Building Blocks: Wildcards and Default Entries
sections.content:
Wildcarding is powerful but subtle. When querying, the actor field is treated literally (no wildcards). When creating or retrieving entries, wildcards are allowed. The service uses a priority scheme: exact matches are best, then wildcard matches with the shortest match string are preferred.

Every owner has four default entries that take effect unless explicitly overridden:

  • local@domain can perform all actions (the owner themselves)
  • apex=*@domain can perform all actions (APEX services in the local domain)
  • apex=*@* can only use the core data service (APEX services anywhere)
  • *@* can perform nothing (everyone else starts forbidden)

This means by default, your own endpoint and local APEX services have full access, while outsiders are denied unless you explicitly grant them permission.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules start with sensible defaults: you can do anything as yourself, APEX services in your domain can do anything, APEX services elsewhere can only send mail, and strangers cannot do anything. You can override any of these.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The access service relies on APEX's authentication mechanisms. The relaying mesh checks access entries when delivering data (RFC 3340, step 5.3), so the access service must be consulted by relays. An originating endpoint can query the service to know its own permissions, and a recipient can modify its own access entries.

One privacy note: timestamps in access entries may disclose location or timezone information. If this is sensitive, administrators can use the special timezone value -00:00 to obscure the local time.
sections.plainLanguage: The access service is an important part of APEX security, because without it, there is no way to say 'no' to someone sending you messages. Timestamps can leak where you are, so you can mask them if needed.
